           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA



         IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF             )
         OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY               )

         SERVICE FOR EXTRA LARGE LOAD                    )

         TO RECOVER COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH                )

                                       REBUTTAL TESTIMONY
                                     OF ADRIAN J. KIMBROUGH




                                    ON BEHALF OF GOOGLE, LLC




                                             October 5, 2026
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 22




                                                  TABLE OF CONTENTS




                       I. INTRODUCTION .......................................................................................... 2

                       II. CONTRACT TERM & LOAD RAMP.......................................................... 3

                       III. PRE-SERVICE RESERVATION CHARGE .............................................. 5

                       IV. CUSTOMER AFFORDABILITY CHARGE .............................................. 7

                       V. CUSTOMER SITE & NETWORK UPGRADES ....................................... 10

                       VI. CUSTOMER CLASS PROTECTION CHARGE..................................... 12

          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                                                1
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 22




    1                                         I.     INTRODUCTION

    2    Q.     Please state your name, business address, and position.

    3    A.     My name is Adrian J. Kimbrough, and my business address is 417 Denison Street,

    4           Highland Park, New Jersey, 08904. I am employed as a Senior Vice President at Gabel

    5           Associates, Inc., an energy, environmental, and public utility consulting firm.

    6    Q.     Are you the same Adrian Kimbrough that provided responsive testimony in this case?

    7    A.     Yes.

    8    Q.     What is the purpose of your testimony?

    9    A.     My rebuttal testimony responds to the testimony of Walmart witness Michael Marchand;

   10           Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers (“OIEC”) witness James R. Dauphinais;

   11           Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (“PAO”) witness David E. Dismukes; Public Utility

   12           Division (“PUD”) witness David Scalf; and Oklahoma Attorney General witnesses Frank

   13           J. Beling and Ryan M. Lewis (collectively, the “Stakeholders”). Their testimony addresses

   14           the scope and design of OG&E’s proposed Extra Large Power and Light (“XLPL”) tariff,

   15           including cost allocation and consumer protections, contract and billing provisions, and

   16           self-supply and generation options.

   17    Q.     What are your conclusions and recommendations?

   18    A.     A properly designed large-load tariff provides an incredible opportunity to encourage

   19           economic growth and its associated benefits while establishing stringent protections for

   20           Oklahoma ratepayers. By anchoring Schedule XLPL firmly to foundational regulatory

   21           principles — specifically strict cost causation, used-and-useful, and non-discrimination —




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                     2
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 22




    1          my proposed modifications eliminate arbitrary cost-shifting, mitigate utility over recovery,

    2          and prevent existing customers from bearing stranded generation and transmission risks.

    3          Rather than exposing retail customers to unhedged utility buildouts or non-cost-based

    4          excise surcharges, my recommendation directly aligns customer obligations with actual

    5          incurred utility costs and introduces viable sleeved self-supply options.

    6                 My recommendation delivers superior protections and affordability benefits for

    7          existing residential and commercial customers compared to OG&E’s proposal, ensuring

    8          that new large loads contribute meaningfully to the grid without eroding rate affordability

    9          for the households and businesses already here. Ultimately, adopting these balanced

   10          revisions achieves a transparent, win-win regulatory standard that reliably protects

   11          everyday customers while positioning Oklahoma as a predictable destination for

   12          substantial commercial investment.

   13                 My recommendations, which remain the same as those presented in my responsive

   14          testimony, are outlined in Exhibit AJK 2.

   15    Q.    Do you have any attachments?

   16    A.    No.

   17                               II. CONTRACT TERM & LOAD RAMP

   18    Q.    Did the Stakeholders address contract term and load ramp?

   19    A.    Yes. The Stakeholders addressed initial terms, extensions, renewals, notice, the five-year

   20          ramp, resource demonstrations, and OG&E’s authority to delay load growth. They agree

   21          that large loads create planning, investment, resource-adequacy, stranded-cost, and cost-




         Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                       3
         Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 22




    1           shifting risks. They generally view a 15-year term for full-requirements service and a five-

    2           year ramp as within peer ranges. Their main dispute concerns whether all customers should

    3           receive the same term and protections. OEIC witness Dauphinais supports a uniform 10-

    4           year term, annual resource demonstrations, and OG&E ramp-delay authority. (Dauphinais,

    5           p. 43, ll. 16–19). PAO witness Dismukes finds a 15-year term within the surveyed range.

    6           (Dismukes, p. 11, ll. 14–16). PUD witness Scalf supports a 15-year term and related

    7           financial protections for Bring Your Own Generation (“BYOG”) customers. (Scalf, p. 41,

    8           ll. 2–11).

    9    Q.     Do the stakeholders’ proposals align contract obligations and ramp protections with

   10           the risks each customer creates?

   11    A.     No. Although the stakeholders raise legitimate concerns, their proposals do not consistently

   12           match contractual protections to the risks each customer creates. Dauphinais’s uniform 10-

   13           year term understates the long-term generation risk associated with full-requirements

   14           service, while his ramp-delay proposal gives OG&E excessive discretion over risks that

   15           may be within its control. Dismukes’s survey supports 15 years as within a peer range but

   16           does not justify identical terms for different service arrangements. (Dismukes, p. 12, ll. 14–

   17           16). Conversely, Scalf’s combination of Contributions in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”),

   18           collateral, minimum bills, exit fees, and a 15-year term risks over-protecting OG&E

   19           without tying each measure to a specific exposure. A 15-year term is also less justified for

   20           the portion of generation costs a customer self-supplies, or dedicated transmission facilities

   21           that a customer funds through CIAC. (Scalf, p. 41, ll. 2–10).




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                         4
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 22




    1    Q.     What contract-term and load-ramp framework should the Commission adopt?

    2    A.     I recommend a 15-year term for full-requirements service and a maximum 10-year term

    3           for customers that self-supply generation and fund dedicated transmission facilities through

    4           CIAC. For customers taking partial supply service from OG&E, meaning some of the

    5           customer generation service will be self supply, the contract term would be between 10 and

    6           15 years, driven by the portion of load self supplied. Longer terms should require

    7           documented, Commission-approved cost support. Service after the initial term should

    8           continue under the tariff with symmetrical 12-month notice. The five-year ramp limit

    9           should remain. Any resource demonstration or ramp delay should follow objective

   10           reliability standards, regulatory oversight, and responsibility-based protections. This

   11           framework aligns each obligation with actual utility exposure and protects both existing

   12           customers and large-load customers.

   13                             III. PRE-SERVICE RESERVATION CHARGE

   14    Q.     What issues do the stakeholders’ positions raise concerning the Pre-Service

   15           Reservation Charge?

   16    A.     The central issue raised by Stakeholders is whether OG&E may collect a monthly $2.50

   17           per kW charge before commercial service begins without demonstrating cost causation.

   18           Dauphinais and Dismukes explain that the charge lacks cost-causation support and should

   19           be rejected, while Beling acknowledges that OG&E provided no substantive basis for the

   20           charge level. (Dauphinais, p. 27, ll. 15–20; Dismukes, p. 18, ll. 1–5, Beling, p. 11, ll. 1–3).

   21           Marchand and Lewis take no position. (Marchand, p. 3, ll. 9–16; Lewis, p. 19, ll. 13–15).




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                          5
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 22




    1           Scalf supports collection for up to 24 months because the proceeds would fund residential

    2           credits, but does not require them to correspond to engineering, capacity-reservation,

    3           carrying, or other identified costs. (Scalf, p. 45, ll. 1–11). Beling would distribute the

    4           proceeds more broadly if the charge is approved, but that changes only the beneficiaries,

    5           not the unsupported foundation. (Beling, p. 11, ll. 4–8). The Commission must therefore

    6           assess the charge’s cost basis, timing, overlap with existing engineering and construction

    7           payments, revenue treatment, and financing benefit to OG&E.

    8    Q.     Why do the proposals that would retain or redistribute the charge fail to resolve its

    9           cost and financing concerns?

   10    A.     Scalf’s reliance on potential pre-service activities and residential benefits does not establish

   11           any actual costs caused by a prospective customer. OG&E already recovers documented

   12           engineering and design expenses through the Preliminary Agreement, while the customer

   13           funds dedicated transmission and substation facilities through CIAC. The Reservation

   14           Charge identifies no separate expense, creating potential overlapping and unnecessary

   15           recovery. The $2.50/kW rate was adopted from OG&E’s residential-affordability proposal

   16           and applied to Maximum Contract Demand to generate $30 million annually per 1,000

   17           MW. It was not derived from engineering, reserved capacity, carrying costs, or another

   18           pre-service study.

   19                   Placing the collections in a regulatory liability for residential credits confirms that

   20           the charge operates as a transfer between customer classes rather than reimbursement for




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                           6
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 22




    1          actual incurred preparation costs. Beling’s broader distribution proposal changes the

    2          beneficiaries but does not cure the charge’s calculation, timing, or duplication defects.

    3                 The proposal also gives OG&E interest-free cash before electricity is delivered,

    4          while the large load customer separately funds engineering and dedicated facilities. No

    5          tariff mechanism credits that financing value to the large load customer or offsets

    6          documented pre-service costs.

    7    Q.    How should the Commission address pre-service costs?

    8    A.    I recommend that the Commission deny and remove the Pre-Service Reservation Charge

    9          in its entirety. OG&E should recover pre-service costs exclusively through verified

   10          engineering, design, and study expenses under the Preliminary Agreement, followed by

   11          dollar-for-dollar reconciliation to actual costs. This approach protects other customers,

   12          compensates OG&E for legitimate work, prevents overlapping recovery, and keeps

   13          prospective-customer obligations tied to documented costs.

   14                           IV. CUSTOMER AFFORDABILITY CHARGE

   15    Q.    What issues do the stakeholders raise concerning the Customer Affordability

   16          Charge?

   17    A.    OG&E proposes a $2.50 per kW-month charge designed to collect $30 million annually

   18          per gigawatt of XLPL demand. Stakeholders question whether the charge reflects XLPL

   19          cost causation, whether benefits should be limited to residential customers, how collections

   20          should be held, and whether another structure would better advance affordability.

   21          Dauphinais, Dismukes, and I recommend rejection because OG&E has not tied the charge




         Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                          7
         Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 22




    1           to XLPL service costs. (Dauphinais, p. 27, ll. 15–20; Dismukes, p. 19, ll. 9–12). Beling

    2           likewise finds no support for the collection target. (Beling, p. 11, ll. 1–3). Scalf would

    3           retain the charge and credit the residential class, while Beling would distribute benefits

    4           among all non-large-load classes. (Scalf, p. 47, ll. 15–17; Beling, p. 11, ll. 4–8). Marchand

    5           and Lewis take no position. (Marchand, p. 3, ll. 9–16; Lewis, p. 19, ll. 13–15).

    6    Q.     Why do the proposals to retain or broaden the charge fail to resolve its underlying

    7           defects?

    8    A.     The proposals leave fundamental defects unresolved. Scalf cites identified residential

    9           program costs to support the charge, but those costs show how OG&E plans to spend the

   10           revenue, not the cost of actually serving XLPL customers. A class-wide residential credit

   11           further weakens the affordability rationale by distributing limited funds without regard to

   12           household need, energy burden, or housing condition. Although Beling correctly identifies

   13           the unsupported $30 million target, broader distribution neither converts an arbitrary

   14           collection into a cost-based rate nor ensures alignment with the stated low-income purpose.

   15           Both proposals also give OG&E interest-free working capital from customer-supplied

   16           funds without a corresponding customer benefit. Finally, both retain a demand-based

   17           charge tied to reserved capacity rather than actual operations.

   18    Q.     What approach should the Commission take if it requires an affordability

   19           contribution?

   20    A.     If the Commission determines that XLPL customers should make a separate affordability

   21           contribution, I recommend replacing OG&E’s proposal with the Oklahoma Energy




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                        8
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 22




    1           Affordability and Energy Efficiency Rider. The rider would assess $0.00075 per metered

    2           kWh after commercial operations begin. A volumetric charge would scale with actual

    3           delivered energy and establish a predictable monthly obligation based on customer

    4           operations. OG&E would serve solely as the billing and collection conduit. It would remit

    5           all proceeds monthly to an independent, segregated account administered by the Oklahoma

    6           Department of Human Services. This structure would eliminate OG&E’s unjust and

    7           unreasonable working-capital windfall, and provide transparent control over the use of the

    8           funds.

    9                    The proceeds should support verified low-income affordability measures, with

   10           priority given to pre-weatherization, structural repairs, building-envelope improvements,

   11           and HVAC upgrades. These measures are directly relevant to affordability because

   12           deteriorated housing conditions and inefficient equipment can produce persistently high

   13           household energy use. Structural repairs and pre-weatherization can prepare homes for

   14           effective efficiency improvements. Envelope and HVAC upgrades can then reduce

   15           consumption and lower bills year after year. This approach creates continuing benefits that

   16           compound over time and directs limited resources to households with demonstrated needs.

   17           Targeted bill stabilization may supplement these investments when immediate assistance

   18           is appropriate. Independent administration would also help ensure that expenditures remain

   19           confined to the Commission’s stated low-income affordability purposes.




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                      9
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 22




    1                           V. CUSTOMER SITE & NETWORK UPGRADES

    2    Q.     What issues do the stakeholders’ proposals raise concerning customer-funded

    3           infrastructure?

    4    A.     The Commission must distinguish dedicated facilities serving one customer from shared

    5           upgrades benefiting multiple users. The stakeholders generally agree that customers should

    6           fund dedicated facilities to prevent subsidies and stranded investment, and Scalf agrees that

    7           CIAC-funded assets must remain outside rate base. (Dauphinais, p. 28, ll. 10–17;

    8           Dismukes, p. 15, ll. 3–6; Scalf, p. 28, ll. 1–4; Lewis, p. 17, ll. 1–6; Scalf, p. 28, ll. 5–8).

    9           They differ on shared facilities and administration. Dismukes and Scalf would broadly

   10           assign infrastructure costs to the XLPL customer without clearly allocating shared benefits.

   11           (Dismukes, p. 15, ll. 3–6; Scalf, p. 28, ll. 1–4). Dauphinais would address rolled-in upgrade

   12           costs through the Customer Class Protection Charge, while Lewis would size contributions

   13           to avoid increasing other classes’ transmission allocations. (Dauphinais, p. 30, ll. 8–14;

   14           Lewis, p. 17, ll. 4–13). These approaches do not consistently measure incremental

   15           causation or benefits. They also omit key protections, including design and procurement

   16           review, self-build rights, alternatives analysis, audits, timely reconciliation, interest-

   17           bearing refunds, later-user reimbursement, and clear rate-base exclusions.

   18    Q.     Why do the proposed funding approaches provide inadequate cost-allocation and

   19           construction safeguards?

   20    A.     A blanket requirement that one customer fund every associated infrastructure cost violates

   21           cost causation when upgrades also benefit existing or future users. The proposals by




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                         10
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 22




    1           Dismukes and Scalf should be rejected to the extent they would assign the paying customer

    2           costs attributable to broader system benefits.

    3                  Dauphinais’s approach is also incomplete because rolling all shared-upgrade costs

    4           into system rates may eliminate the triggering customer’s responsibility for costs its load

    5           caused. A later class-cost study cannot determine causal responsibility or discern project

    6           scope. Lewis supports partial prefunding, but his “hold other classes harmless” formula

    7           may obscure engineering causation and long-term capacity benefits. Allocation should

    8           begin with the incremental costs caused by the customer, with remaining costs assigned

    9           according to quantified benefits under a Commission-approved framework.

   10                  Construction safeguards may also be necessary when a customer funding a

   11           dedicated facility bears the consequences of OG&E’s decisions. Tariff protections should

   12           govern design, procurement, audits, reconciliation, refunds, and later-user reimbursement.

   13           Finally, customer advances and CIAC must be excluded from rate base and capital

   14           structure to prevent duplicate recovery. Proposals lacking that binding protection should

   15           be rejected.

   16    Q.     What protections should govern customer-funded infrastructure?

   17    A.     I recommend tariff language that: assigns 100 percent CIAC only to dedicated facilities

   18           providing no material system benefit; grants design review, procurement review, audit, and

   19           qualified self-build rights; allocates shared-upgrade costs by incremental causation and

   20           quantified benefits; requires lower-cost alternatives analysis; reconciles deposits to verified

   21           as-built costs within 90 days and refunds excess collections with interest; reimburses the




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                         11
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 13 OF 22




    1           original funder when later customers use funded capacity; and excludes every customer-

    2           funded asset, advance, and prepayment from rate base and capital structure. These

    3           protections apply cost causation consistently and prevent overcollection, free-riding, and

    4           duplicate recovery.

    5                           VI. CUSTOMER CLASS PROTECTION CHARGE

    6    Q.     What issues do the Stakeholders’ proposed customer-protection mechanisms raise?

    7    A.     The issue is whether the Commission should authorize a recurring class-level protection

    8           charge, regulatory accounts, or other true-up mechanisms before the XLPL class develops

    9           an operating history. The witnesses generally agree that existing customers should be

   10           protected from costs caused by XLPL service and that any analysis must account for the

   11           large load, associated service costs, and relevant revenues. (Dauphinais, p. 37, ll. 12–19;

   12           Scalf, p. 54, ll. 1–5; Lewis, p. 16, ll. 4–7; Beling, p. 12, ll. 13–20).

   13                   The Stakeholders differ on mechanism design. Dauphinais supports a symmetrical

   14           class-level comparison; Dismukes proposes a replacement System Impact Charge with

   15           periodic Fuel Cost Adjustment (“FCA”) credits; Scalf recommends annual assessments,

   16           FCA review, regulatory accounts, and later rate-case disposition; Beling supports a

   17           recurring class-level fail-safe; and Lewis proposes a true-up for Construction Work In

   18           Progress (“CWIP”) timing. (Dauphinais, p. 40, ll. 3–25; Dismukes, p. 5, ll. 14–16, p. 16,

   19           ll. 1–4; Scalf, p. 29, ll. 13–20; Beling, p. 12, ll. 1–3; Lewis, p. 18, ll. 7–12). I recommend

   20           customer-specific review using actual, audited data in a general rate case, with any

   21           demonstrated deficiency corrected prospectively through base rates.




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                        12
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 14 OF 22




    1    Q.     Why do the proposed recurring reviews and true-ups fail to provide a reliable or

    2           reasonable remedy?

    3    A.     The proposals assume harm before XLPL develops reliable usage, revenue, peak-demand,

    4           and cost data. They are therefore inconsistent with cost-causation, used-and-useful, non-

    5           discrimination, and just-and-reasonable principles requiring demonstrated costs and

    6           substantial evidence.

    7                  Dauphinais avoids retroactive ratemaking but relies on class-level aggregation that

    8           may shift costs among materially different customers. Dismukes adds FCA credits without

    9           a complete method for matching actual costs, revenues, overcollections, and

   10           undercollections. Scalf’s annual reviews and regulatory accounts would require recurring

   11           litigation and record adverse impacts without symmetrical treatment of benefits. Beling’s

   12           portfolio-level fail-safe may obscure customer-specific costs, CIAC, operating

   13           characteristics, and system benefits. Lewis identifies a potential CWIP timing issue but

   14           provides no comprehensive method for evaluating total revenues, usage, CIAC, allocation

   15           factors, and benefits.

   16                  These issues could consume substantial Commission and stakeholder resources

   17           without establishing that a charge is necessary or accurately targeted. A general rate case

   18           provides audited data, a complete system record, customer-specific analysis, and

   19           prospective correction through established ratemaking.




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                     13
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 15 OF 22




    1    Q.     How should the Commission evaluate and correct any demonstrated cost deficiency?

    2    A.     I recommend that the Commission reject the Customer Class Protection Charge and annual

    3           net-cost true-ups. OG&E should present any cost-impact concerns or findings in a general

    4           rate case using actual, audited data and customer-specific analysis. The analysis should

    5           include associated service costs, billing revenues, customer-funded CIAC, and verified

    6           ratemaking related system benefits. Any demonstrated deficiency should be addressed on

    7           a prospective basis. This approach protects existing customers, preserves billing finality,

    8           applies long-standing regulatory principles, and avoids recurring administrative reviews

    9           and litigation.

   10                                                VII. SELF-SUPPLY

   11    Q.     What issues do the stakeholders’ self-supply proposals raise?

   12    A.     The central issue is whether Rate Schedule XLPL should offer standardized full and partial

   13           self-supply for customers using third-party or customer-owned generation while remaining

   14           OG&E retail customers. OG&E proposes only bundled service, leaving self-supply to

   15           individual negotiation and exposing its captive retail customers to stranded cost risks.

   16                   Dauphinais, Dismukes, and Scalf agree that self-supply can reduce OG&E’s

   17           resource obligations and stranded-cost risk. (Dismukes, p. 18, ll. 8–15; Dauphinais, p. 5,

   18           ll. 37–43 and p. 49, ll. 17–22; Scalf, p. 40, ll. 1–8 and p. 43, ll. 7–14). Scalf further agrees

   19           that OG&E should remove generation-related charges for self-supplied requirements,

   20           while Beling supports defined eligibility, SPP qualification, and customer-risk protections.




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                          14
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 16 OF 22




    1           This agreement amongst parties supports approving tariffed self-supply now. (Scalf, p. 41,

    2           ll. 1–3; Beling, p. 23, ll. 21–23; p. 24, ll. 1–2).

    3                   The parties differ primarily on timing, resource control, and continuing obligations.

    4           Dauphinais would defer BYOG to a later proceeding; Scalf would approve it through a

    5           compliance filing but retain a 15-year term, collateral, exit fees, affordability charges, and

    6           delivery-related minimums. (Dauphinais, p. 50, ll. 3–8; Scalf, p. 48, ll. 14–21; Scalf, p. 41,

    7           ll. 2–11). Beling’s Accelerated Capacity Support (“ACS”) proposal instead transfers

    8           planning capacity to OG&E, subject to utility need, evaluation, and approval. It is

    9           customer-assisted utility procurement, not self-supply, because customers retain no

   10           wholesale supply election, generation-charge offset, hourly power purchase agreement

   11           (“PPA”) settlement, or right to serve full or partial load. (Beling, p. 19, ll. 10–19; p. 22, ll.

   12           10–23; p. 23, ll. 1–7).

   13                   My proposal provides true self-supply and is the only proposal that shields captive

   14           retail customers from stranded costs: customers retain, finance, and bear the risks of their

   15           generation arrangements while paying OG&E for delivery, supplemental generation, and

   16           documented incremental administration. It best protects Oklahoma ratepayers while

   17           supporting long-term economic development.

   18    Q.     Why do the proposed deferral, retained obligations, and utility-controlled

   19           alternatives fail to provide true self-supply?




          Rebuttal Testimony – Adrian J. Kimbrough                                                          15
          Case No. PUD 2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 62 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 17 OF 22




    1    A.     The opposing proposals conflict with the economic premise of self-supply, retain

    2           obligations associated with risks that the customer has already removed, and fail to protect

    3           captive retail customers from stranded costs.

    4                    Deferral to a new proceeding is unreasonable. The record establishes the need for

    5           full and partial self-supply and identifies the required protections. Rider Self Supply

    6           Service (“Rider SSS”) provides eligibility, accreditation, reserve-margin, telemetry,

    7           scheduling, billing, settlement, and cost-allocation rules. Dauphinais supports BYOG

    8           because it can eliminate OG&E’s need to acquire production resources, yet his procedural

    9           recommendation postpones the mechanism that produces that protection. A delay merely

   10           preserves the very generation investment and stranded-cost exposure his proposal seeks to

   11           avoid.

   12                    Scalf supports self-supply because a customer-supplied resource avoids OG&E

   13           generation costs. His proposal then retains a 15-year term, collateral, exit fees, affordability

   14           charges, and minimum-billing obligations. Those requirements were designed principally
